extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, logicians, and advanced students interested in formalism and foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and critiquing variants of formalism (Hilbertian, game, term, Curry-Howard based, nominalist) by examining their ability to meet demands such as consistency, applicability, ontological neutrality, metatheoretical adequacy, and extensions of correspondences like Curry–Howard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contentful conservative extension result
rubrics_metrics.description: We need a contentful conservative extension result to show that for the calculi we do use, no disaster can occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one stipulates bridge principles (e.g. linking numerals to sentences about counts) and adds arithmetic rules, one must show via a conservative extension result—preferably a contentful truth rather than merely a derivable string—that the richer system does not introduce disastrous consequences for the intended calculus. Anti-pattern: accepting only syntactic derivability without showing contentful conservativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency proof requirement for formalism
rubrics_metrics.description: To vindicate a formalist interpretation and show calculi do not have empirical content, one needs to give a consistency proof for mathematical calculi (Hilbert's aim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gödel’s second theorem complicates this by showing a sufficiently strong system cannot prove its own consistency under natural characterisations; a formalist must address this limitation (e.g. by moving to a stronger language or employing non-finitary techniques) and justify any such moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of Gödelian non-determinate sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalism must confront Gödel’s incompleteness theorems which yield arithmetical sentences neither provable nor refutable (non-determinate sentences) and explain their status, especially if some such sentences are nonetheless true in the standard model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include adopting stronger rules such as the ω-rule to make true arithmetic sentences provable relative to a weak finitary logic, or explaining how non-determinate sentences fit into the framework; the account must avoid implausible consequences (e.g. large classes of true but unprovable sentences left unexplained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of non-finitary metamathematical techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: If one uses metamathematical techniques that are not finitary (e.g. rules with infinitely many premises), the formalist must justify the acceptability of such methods relative to their philosophical aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carnap used infinitary devices (the ω-rule) and other non-finitary tools; the formalist must explain why employing such methods does not undermine the anti-epistemological/finitary motivation of formalism or otherwise concede unwanted commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of applicability (applicability problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalism must explain how mathematics can be applicable to the empirical world—how applied mathematical notions (e.g. 'the number of φs') obtain meaning when mathematics and empirical language are combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plausible strategy should reconcile a proof-theoretic (syntactic) semantics for pure mathematics with a (perhaps realist) truth-conditional semantics for empirical language; anti-pattern: declaring ontological neutrality while failing to account for pragmatic success in application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic justification for framework choice (Principle of Tolerance)
rubrics_metrics.description: External questions about which linguistic/framework to adopt are to be answered by decisions based on pragmatic criteria regarding the efficiency, fruitfulness and utility of the framework with respect to the aims of the discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formalists invoking Principle of Tolerance must clarify what the aims are and show that pragmatic criteria adequately ground framework selection rather than covert metaphysical commitments. Beware treating ontological neutrality as a sham when pragmatic aims tacitly presuppose empiricist furniture (e.g. sense data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust account of ontological neutrality
rubrics_metrics.description: Formalism’s claim that ‘correctness’ is determined by the rules of a system and not by correspondence with an independent realm of facts must be sustained without simply shifting ontological commitments into metamathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The formalist should show that rejecting framework-transcendent distinctions genuinely dissolves ontological worries, and must address worries about how finite agents can have knowledge of putatively abstract domains; anti-pattern: claiming neutrality while embracing commitments (e.g. infinite ontologies) implicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure and formation guarantees for nominalist syntax
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominalist/formalist attempts to treat mathematical expressions as concrete marks must provide guarantees (not hand-waving 'and so on') that their definitions ensure closure under formation for arbitrary complex formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goodman and Quine's approach faces a gap in moving from finite cases to arbitrary formulas without an available induction principle; criterion: present a method (or justify reliance on resources) that secures closure for arbitrary formula complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of extremely large/complex sentences and proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A nominalist formalism must account for sentences (tokens) for which no concrete proof or refutation could exist in practice (e.g. enormous number-theoretic statements), and decide whether such sentences are true, false, or indeterminate in their framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implausible conclusions (e.g. declaring many decidable sentences neither true nor false); provide a coherent stance on existence of concrete proofs versus abstract provability and implications for mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous specification of what counts as formal system/tokens
rubrics_metrics.description: Term formalists must give a rigorous account of what a formal system is and what the primitive 'tokens' or expression-types are, including whether these are to be taken syntactically, meta-syntactically or as abstract/non-syntactic entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curry attempts a precise account but must address whether treating mathematics as metamathematics collapses mathematical practice into statements about expression strings; criterion: explain how typical mathematical investigations about sets, spaces, functions, etc., are accommodated within the proposed ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of the metatheory and its ontological commitments
rubrics_metrics.description: Any formalist stance must address the metatheory: what resources (e.g. countable ontology, choice principles, set-theoretic assumptions) are needed to state and prove meta-theorems, and what ontological commitments do these involve?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrations that appeal to generalisations over all numbers or selections may presuppose principles (induction, choice) unavailable to strict nominalists; the account should either justify these presuppositions or show how to avoid them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Curry–Howard correspondences to ground correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The CH correspondence linking propositions and types (proofs and programs) can be used by formalists to identify correctness with provability (or type inhabitation); a formalist should exploit this correspondence where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: links proofs to computations, supports syntactico-semantics, and provides programmatic evaluations via normalization. Limitations: must generalize CH beyond intuitionistic/propositional fragments to classical logic, richer systems, and non-constructive mathematics if one wishes non-revisionism; also address issues about abstractness of proofs as types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalisation/evaluation metatheory
rubrics_metrics.description: A good proof-theoretic/type-theoretic account should have a normalisation metatheorem (proof reduction to normal form) and a correspondence between normalisation and program evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property supports the identification of proofs with computational processes and helps ground syntactico-semantics; criterion: show normalization holds (or state its limits) for the systems claimed to underpin formalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of classical logic and primeness/excluded middle
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensions of CH-style formalism to classical logics face problems such as lack of primeness (when ⊢ A ∨ B but neither ⊢ A nor ⊢ B), which complicates identifying correctness with provability and justifying excluded middle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A formalist must either supply technical work to generalize CH correspondences to classical/other logics, or provide philosophical justification (e.g. supervaluationist strategies) for using classical reasoning within a provability-based correctness concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance or justification of abstract metamathematical objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Anti‑platonist formalists must show how to avoid commitment to abstract objects (e.g. infinitely many proofs/types) that arise in syntactico-semantics or CH-based readings, or else justify why such commitments are acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If proofs/types are taken as abstract objects, then the anti‑platonist motivation is undermined; the formalist needs either a strategy to reconstruct metatheory concretely or an account that explains why abstract commitments do not threaten the philosophical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of 'ideal' parts of mathematics (undecidable zones)
rubrics_metrics.description: A contemporary (Hilbertian) formalist must decide how to treat undecidable branches (e.g. CH, GCH): as 'ideal' parts lacking content, as legitimately part of mathematics, or otherwise, and explain the practical and philosophical consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some mathematicians treat such areas as lacking content (Cohen, Robinson). A satisfactory formalism should justify this classification and clarify implications for mathematical practice and ontology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between informal proofs and indicated formal derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: If ordinary informal mathematical proofs are said to 'indicate' formal derivations (Azzouni), the formalist must explicate the indication relation: whether indicated derivations must exist, whether they belong to a single system or a family, and how non-existent or very long derivations can ground mathematical consensus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an account that avoids opaque appeals to nonexistent derivations as explanatory devices, or show how such a family-of-derivations view plausibly explains mathematicians' reliability; anti-pattern: leaving the indication relation vague and explanatorily empty.
